strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in audio-text retrieval evaluation: the mismatch between caption-style benchmark queries and realistic user search behavior (questions, commands, tags, paraphrases, exclusions).

Contributes a well-structured UIQ taxonomy (Conversational, Reformulation, Exclusionary) and releases three benchmark datasets (AudioCaps-UIQ, Clotho-UIQ, MECAT-UIQ) with both human and LLM-based quality validation.

Proposes novel and well-motivated discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, ∆-Rank) that go beyond standard R@k to explicitly measure suppression of acoustically similar but semantically distinct hard negatives, illustrated clearly via Figure 3.

Conducts a rigorous and unusually thorough data-leakage analysis between WavCaps and AudioCaps/Clotho (17.7% and 61.0% overlap respectively), and appropriately introduces MECAT as a leakage-free evaluation set — a valuable methodological contribution to the field.

Extensive experimentation across three backbones (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/7B), multiple datasets, and many query types, with detailed appendices covering implementation, efficiency, prompts, and additional metrics, supporting reproducibility.
Reports results honestly, including cases where OEA underperforms M2D-CLAP (standard T2A, Question/Keyphrase/Paraphrase UIQ types), rather than overstating uniform superiority.
weaknesses: The headline T2T 'dominance' result is somewhat unsurprising and possibly not an apples-to-apples comparison: an LLM backbone with billions of parameters is compared against CLAP's lightweight text towers on a text-to-text task, which is a different setting from the paper's stated audio-text retrieval goal; the practical relevance of this caption-based pipeline (requiring an additional, unevaluated audio-captioning step) is not empirically validated end-to-end.

Absolute hard-negative discrimination performance remains low for all models (HNSR@10 around 30-35%), so while the reported relative improvement is notable, the practical significance of 'substantially superior' discrimination is questionable given both models still fail on the majority of exclusionary queries.

UIQ benchmark quality validation relies on a small sample (75 audio clips, 675 ratings) relative to the full 13,053-query benchmark, and queries are generated by a single LLM (GPT-5.1) under vocabulary-grounding constraints, raising concerns about diversity and representativeness that are only partially mitigated by length-distribution comparisons to real Freesound queries.

The hard negative mining pipeline is seeded by MGA-CLAP embeddings and filtered by BGE, which are the same models being compared against or closely related in spirit to baselines used in the discrimination evaluation, creating some circularity risk that human verification only partially addresses.

Results do not scale monotonically with backbone size (7B does not consistently outperform 3B, and even underperforms Nemo3B on some MECAT metrics), which weakens the narrative that larger/more capable LLM backbones straightforwardly translate to better retrieval-relevant semantic understanding.

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported for the reported percentage-point and relative-improvement claims, making it hard to assess whether differences (e.g., +4.3%p HNSR@10) are robust versus noise across query/backbone variants.

OEA's efficiency profile is substantially worse than CLAP baselines (10-20x more GPU memory, several-fold higher latency), which is acknowledged but somewhat understates the practical deployment cost trade-off relative to the modest average performance gains.

The core modeling contribution (LoRA-tuned multimodal LLM backbone as a unified dual-purpose text/audio embedding model) is architecturally incremental relative to existing text-embedding-from-LLM approaches, with the paper's novelty concentrated more in the benchmark/metrics than the model itself.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in audio-text retrieval evaluation: standard benchmarks use caption-style queries that do not reflect real-world search behavior, and the paper systematically motivates this with prior literature (Weck & Font, Selvakumar et al.).

Introduces and releases three new UIQ benchmark datasets (AudioCaps-UIQ, Clotho-UIQ, MECAT-UIQ) spanning five query formulations, along with code, checkpoints, and a web demo, providing a useful community resource.

Rigorous data-leakage analysis (Appendix B) quantifying WavCaps overlap with AudioCaps (17.7%) and Clotho (61.0%) test sets is a valuable and often-overlooked methodological contribution, and the use of MECAT as a leakage-free benchmark strengthens the evaluation's validity.
Proposes well-motivated discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, ∆-Rank) that expose a real blind spot of standard R@k metrics for exclusionary queries, illustrated clearly (Figure 3).

Extensive and unusually self-critical mechanism ablations (Appendix O) that decompose the source of OEA's hard-negative discrimination gains via controlled experiments (audio-only separation, negation on/off, word-shuffle controls, cross-model shuffle controls) with proper paired statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank), leading the authors to revise/qualify their own hypothesis rather than overclaim.
Reasonably broad experimental coverage: three backbones, four CLAP baselines, three evaluation datasets, and detailed per-query-type breakdowns in the appendix.
UIQ benchmark quality is validated with both human annotation and LLM-based scoring, with reported inter-rater/agreement statistics.
weaknesses: The architecture itself (shared LLM backbone + LoRA adapters + modality-specific projection heads trained with symmetric InfoNCE) is a relatively straightforward application of existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning and contrastive learning techniques, offering limited technical/methodological novelty.

The headline T2T improvement (+22%) is a somewhat unfair/expected comparison: CLAP's lightweight text encoders were never designed for text-to-text semantic matching, so an LLM backbone naturally excels here; this result says more about using an LLM as a sentence encoder than about audio-text retrieval per se.

Core T2A retrieval results show only "comparable" performance to M2D-CLAP (and worse on AudioCaps specifically), while OEA's inference cost is substantially higher (audio encoding latency 164–667 ms/clip vs. 30–108 ms/clip for CLAP baselines, per Appendix K), raising questions about the practical value of the proposed approach despite the reported gains.

The magnitude of the hard-negative discrimination improvement (+4.3pp HNSR@10) is modest, and the mechanism ablations ultimately show that OEA's text-side order sensitivity is not a unique or novel mechanism but a general property shared with (and in one case weaker than) CLAP baselines — undercutting the strength of the discrimination claim as a distinguishing contribution.

UIQ benchmark quality validation is based on a very small sample (75 of 13,053 queries, ~0.6%), and both the generation (GPT-5.1) and validation (Claude Opus 4.5) rely on proprietary, potentially non-reproducible/non-static LLMs, raising reproducibility concerns and some circularity in using an LLM to validate LLM-generated content.

No empirical comparison of UIQ query statistics (e.g., token length distributions) against real-world query logs (e.g., Freesound queries), despite motivating the work with exactly this kind of mismatch; the connection to genuine real-world search behavior remains largely assumed rather than demonstrated.

The hard-negative mining pipeline depends on MGA-CLAP for candidate retrieval, which is also one of the evaluated baselines, creating a potential circularity/confound that the paper acknowledges but only partially mitigates through threshold calibration rather than independent validation.

Statistical significance for the main comparative results (Tables 2–4) is not reported, in contrast to the appendix ablations which do include significance testing; this makes it harder to assess whether some of the smaller headline gaps (e.g., UIQ category differences) are robust.
